questions.question: For open subsets $(\boldsymbol{E}_i)_{i = 1}^{\infty}$ of a metric space, what does the proposition say about $\bigcup_{i = 1}^{\infty}\boldsymbol{E}_i$?
options: It is closed but not open.
It is open only if the sets are finite.

questions.question: For open subsets $\boldsymbol{E}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{E}_k$, what does the proposition say about $\bigcap_{i = 1}^{k}\boldsymbol{E}_i$?
options: It is necessarily closed but not open.

questions.question: In a metric space $\boldsymbol{X}$, which of the following is always open?
In $\mathbb{R}$, what is $\bigcup_{n = 1}^{\infty}(0,1-\frac{1}{n})$?
Which operation on open sets is guaranteed to preserve openness only in the finite case in the proposition?
Which stronger statement is true for open sets?
options: Any intersection of open sets is open, even for uncountable families.
Any union of open sets is open, even for uncountable families.
Only finite unions of open sets are open.
Open sets are preserved only under pairwise unions.

questions.question: In $\mathbb{R}$, what does the $\bigcap_{n = 1}^{\infty}(-\frac{1}{n},1+\frac{1}{n}) = [0,1]$ show?
options: A finite intersection of open sets can sometimes fail to be open.
A countable union of open sets can fail to be open.
An infinite intersection of open sets can fail to be open.

questions.question: If $\boldsymbol{E}_1,\boldsymbol{E}_2,\boldsymbol{E}_3$ are open subsets of a metric space, what can be concluded about $\boldsymbol{E}_1\cap\boldsymbol{E}_2\cap\boldsymbol{E}_3$?
options: It is not open unless the sets are disjoint.
It is closed but not open.

questions.question: Which word cannot be dropped from the statement that intersections of open sets are open?
Why is the statement about unions of open sets stronger than merely countable unions?
options: It only works for two open sets.
It requires every open set in the family to be bounded as well.
It remains true for arbitrary, even uncountable, families.
It says that every intersection is open.

questions.question: A student claims that $\bigcap_{n = 1}^{\infty}(-\frac{1}{n},1+\frac{1}{n})$ is open because every set in the intersection is open. What is the error?
options: The theorem only guarantees finite intersections of open sets.
Openness is never preserved by intersections, not even for two sets.

questions.question: Let $(\boldsymbol{U}_\alpha)_{\alpha\in A}$ be an arbitrary family of open subsets of a metric space. What can be concluded about $\bigcup_{\alpha\in A}\boldsymbol{U}_\alpha$?
options: It is open only if $A$ is countable.
It is closed but not open.
It is open only if every $\boldsymbol{U}_\alpha$ is non-empty.

questions.question: Which operation preserves openness for any family of open sets?
Which intersection of open sets is guaranteed to be open?
options: Only a countable intersection of closed sets

questions.question: Which two sets are always open in a metric space?
Let $U$ and $V$ be non-empty open proper subsets of $\mathbb R$. Which claim is false?
If $(U_i)_{i=1}^{\infty}$ are open, what can be concluded about $\bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty}U_i$?
In $\mathbb{R}$, what is $\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}(0,1-1/n)$?
Why is the word finite important for intersections of open sets?
options: Finite intersections of open sets may sometimes fail to be open.
The empty set is not open.
Infinite intersections of open sets may fail to be open.
